text: ServiceNow's server-side scripts didn't always look like modern JavaScript, and there's a real engine history behind that. This lesson covers the server-side JavaScript engine itself - where it came from, what changed, and what that means for the code you'll actually read on real instances in the field.

For most of ServiceNow's history, every server-side script ran on Mozilla Rhino, a Java-based JavaScript engine embedded directly in the platform, that only understood ECMAScript 5, the 2009 version of the language. No let, no const, no arrow functions, no template literals, no classes. This example uses var and string concatenation because, under Rhino, that was the only option available - not because anyone chose an old style on purpose.

Around the Quebec release, ServiceNow swapped Rhino for a GraalVM-based engine called GraalJS, running in what's called Rhino-compatibility mode. That means the engine itself is modern and understands ES6 and later, while still preserving Rhino's exact runtime behavior so millions of lines of existing customer scripts across every instance keep working unchanged. Here's the same GlideRecord loop, rewritten with const and a template literal - fully valid today, and it behaves identically to the older version.

It's worth being precise about the boundary. The syntax of the language moved forward - you can now write let, const, arrow functions, and classes in server-side scripts. The platform's own API objects, though, GlideRecord, GlideSystem, and every other Glide object, did not change at all. Same method names, same behavior, on the new engine. That's exactly why most real instances are still full of ES5-style code: it was written before the migration, it still works, and nobody has gone back to rewrite working code just to modernize its syntax. You need to read both styles comfortably, every single day on the job.

Next, we'll look at scope and the this keyword - where var and let behave differently, and why this inside a callback can quietly point somewhere you didn't expect, a bug pattern you will run into constantly in real Script Includes.
